title: A gait foundation model for prediction of multisystem health phenotypes from 3D skeletal motion
desc: Gait is increasingly recognized as a vital sign, yet current approaches treat it as a symptom of specific pathologies rather than a systemic biomarker. Here we developed a gait foundation model for three-dimensional skeletal motion, which was recorded via a single-depth camera during 5 motor tasks, from 3,328 deeply phenotyped adults. Our purpose was to capture the full pattern of a person’s movement and use it to predict health phenotypes such as grip strength and sleep quality across 18 body systems. Gait is conventionally described by engineered features (for example, calculated measurements such as cadence and stride length), which may fail to capture the fine detail of how a person moves. Our model instead translates movement into learned embeddings: sets of numbers that describe how all body joints move together over time. Learned embeddings outperformed engineered features for prediction of age (Pearsonʼs r = 0.69), body mass index ( r = 0.91) and visceral adipose tissue area ( r = 0.83), and embeddings significantly predicted 1,887 of 3,210 tested phenotypes. Relative to a baseline model using age, body mass index, visceral adipose tissue and height alone, gait embeddings improved prediction in all 18 systems in males and 17 of 18 in females, as well as prediction of clinical diagnoses and medication use. Anatomical ablation analyses revealed that leg dynamics dominated metabolic and frailty predictions, and torso dynamics encoded sleep and lifestyle phenotypes. These findings establish gait as an independent, multisystem biosignal, motivating integration of gait analysis into routine clinical assessment as a scalable, passive vital sign. A gait foundation model, developed using three-dimensional skeletal motion data from 3,328 adults, predicts a wide array of clinical characteristics and diagnoses, including cardiometabolic, mental health and frailty phenotypes.

title: A statistical framework for evaluating the repeatability and reproducibility of large language models.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] Systematic evaluation of variability in large language model (LLM)-generated outputs is critical for assessing their reliability. We developed a general statistical framework and Python package (llmReproScore) for quantifying the repeatability and reproducibility of LLM outputs. Following US Food and Drug Administration terminology, our framework establishes four metrics for quantifying LLM repeatability and reproducibility along two dimensions: semantic and internal. Semantic metrics quantify variability in the meaning of LLM-generated outputs, whereas internal metrics quantify variability in token-generation certainty. We validated these metrics, and as an illustrative use case, applied them to diagnostic reasoning outputs generated across LLMs and prompting strategies using US Medical Licensing Examination questions and 90 real-world rare disease cases from the Undiagnosed Diseases Network. Validation results showed that semantic scores aligned with human ratings (Spearman ρ = 0.88 for repeatability and 0.66 for reproducibility) and confirmed that internal metrics capture variability in token-generation certainty. In the illustrative use case, LLM repeatability was generally not associated with accuracy, suggesting that LLM output variability and accuracy capture distinct dimensions of model performance. The proposed metrics can be used to characterize LLM output variability and systematically compare models, prompts, and generation settings. These comparisons can inform more rigorous selection of LLM configurations based on repeatability and reproducibility. We developed and validated generalizable metrics for quantifying LLM output variability. The proposed metrics can complement accuracy-based evaluation to inform experimental design and support more rigorous comparison and selection of models, prompts, and generation settings.

title: Effective trialing of digital interventions in daily life – the mental health perspective
desc: Digital mental health interventions show promise but have yet to meet expectations. We discuss gaps between promising results of pilot studies and null findings in randomized controlled trials, focusing on two major approaches: just-in-time relapse prevention and just-in-time adaptive interventions. We propose that relapse prevention will profit from long-term studies capturing emerging episodes, and we suggest a novel framework for adaptive interventions including causality testing to proceed towards effective trialing.

title: Automated Radiation Target Contouring and Treatment Planning Via RATA: A Multi-Center RCT
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: zhaoxiaohui; conditions: Cancer, Malignant Neoplasms, Radiotherapy; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 62; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Radiotherapy, a cornerstone of comprehensive cancer treatment, relies heavily on clinician expertise for target volume contouring and treatment planning. Consequently, clinical practice is often constrained by procedural bottlenecks, inter-observer variability, and prolonged iterative feedback cycles. Although current artificial intelligence (AI) models have demonstrated progress in automated contouring, key limitations persist, including insufficient integration of multimodal clinical text, a lack of closed-loop dosimetric feedback, and limited generalizability across complex cancer types. This study aims to develop and validate RATA (Radiotherapy Treatment Multi-Agent Assistant), a novel large model system powered by a collaborative multi-agent architecture. Driven by Large Language Model (LLM) decision engines, RATA processes pathological imaging, electronic health records (EHR), and multimodal medical data to construct a end-to-end, fully automated closed-loop pipeline encompassing "target contouring, plan design, dosimetric evaluation, and reflective refinement." Innovatively breaking through traditional unidirectional radiotherapy workflows, the system establishes a dosimetric feedback-driven adaptive iteration mechanism, leveraging dose distribution outcomes to guide multi-agent dynamic fine-tuning of target volumes, thereby mimicking the collaborative clinical logic between senior radiation oncologists and medical physicists. For validation, this study adopts a multi-center, three-stage clinical validation framework-comprising multi-center retrospective validation, human-AI collaborative efficacy assessment, and a prospective randomized controlled trial (RCT)-to comprehensively evaluate the system's performance in improving contouring precision, mitigating experience-dependent disparities across clinician seniority, and reducing total workflow processing time. Implementation of the RATA platform holds potential to eliminate redundant operational steps, enabling a minute-level "scan-to-treat" response. Furthermore, its natural language interaction interface optimizes human-AI collaboration and substantially reduces clinical workload. Overall, this study not only establishes a standardized, intelligent assistance paradigm for precision radiation oncology but also provides essential evidence-based support and technological foundations for the clinical translation of multimodal AI in complex cancer management.

title: Wetter's Digital Twin: A Patient-Specific Framework for Artificial Intelligence and Healthcare.
source: PubMed · JSLS : Journal of the Society of Laparoendoscopic Surgeons
desc: [JSLS : Journal of the Society of Laparoendoscopic Surgeons] The concept of ORReady began with a simple goal: to better prepare the patient, surgeon, operating team, and operating room (OR) environment to improve surgical outcomes. Advances in artificial intelligence, large datasets, electronic health records, imaging, physiological monitoring, wearable technologies, and predictive analytics now create an opportunity to take that concept considerably further. Digital twins, originally developed in engineering, use evolving virtual representations of physical systems to model performance and test possible interventions before they are applied. We propose Wetter's Digital Twin (WDT) as an individualized, dynamic model of the patient that integrates personal health information with artificial intelligence, medical knowledge, and relevant population data. Unlike the conventional medical record, which primarily documents what has occurred, WDT would help clinicians understand what may happen next and explore how different interventions might alter that course. In surgery, such a model could assist with preoperative optimization, procedure selection and planning, intraoperative decision support, and postoperative recovery. The concept, however, extends beyond surgery. The same longitudinal patient-specific model could contribute to prevention, diagnosis, medical treatment, chronic disease management, rehabilitation, and long-term health planning. WDT is proposed not as a replacement for physician judgment or patient participation, but as a means of making increasingly complex health information more useful to both. Important challenges involving data integration, validation, privacy, security, bias, regulation, and clinical responsibility remain. The transition from a medical record that primarily records the past toward a patient-specific model that can also evaluate possible futures may represent an important next step in healthcare.

title: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records
desc: Using electronic health record (EHR) data to answer clinical research questions is challenging. It requires understanding the research question, finding relevant information across different sources, and combining that information to produce meaningful results. We developed an agentic large language model (LLM) pipeline that decomposes investigator-authored requests into source-specific tasks, generates and executes SQL on EHR, integrates structured and unstructured EHR evidence, and applies study-specific clinical note adjudication. We evaluated this workflow against data analyst-identified cohorts across 50 pediatric orthopedic clinical data query requests. Of these, 43 were included in manual-review-adjusted performance analyses. The median adjusted positive predictive value, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach, and corresponding F1 score were 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88-0.98), 0.92 (95% CI, 0.90-0.95) and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.94), respectively. These findings support the feasibility of translating natural-language research intent into executable, autonomous multi-stage EHR workflows.

title: MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term Medical Dialogue
desc: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks the patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text; a patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question. On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.

title: Organotchi: an open-source tool for the automated segmentation, morphological characterization, and longitudinal tracking of organoids
desc: Neural organoids are three-dimensional stem cell-derived models widely used to study brain development and model disease. Brightfield imaging offers a non-invasive readout of their growth and morphology, and recent advances have made automated organoid segmentation from such images increasingly attainable. Yet existing tools largely leave morphological characterization, quality assessment, and comparisons between conditions to manual or ad hoc analysis. Here we present Organotchi, an open-source tool that integrates automated segmentation with longitudinal morphological analysis of neural organoids. Organotchi quantifies ten morphological features, including area, perimeter, and eccentricity, and tracks cystic structures over time, reports variability within and between batches, and flags outlier organoids and segmentation failures, supporting objective organoid characterization and enhancing downstream analysis. As a proof of concept, we apply Organotchi to disease modelling, pharmacological perturbation, and protocol optimization in neural organoids. One use case assesses drug response in breast cancer spheroids, demonstrating its use beyond its development domain.

title: Patient-Friendly Simplifications of Outpatient Reports Using Large Language Models via Few-Shot Prompting: Blinded Comparative Evaluation.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] Effective communication between clinicians and patients plays an important role in the successful delivery of health care. In geriatric medicine, where multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and functional limitations often make treatment plans complex, AI simplifications of clinical reports into patient-friendly language offer a promising way to improve communication. This study investigated whether AI could generate patient-friendly simplifications of outpatient reports that were comparable to those authored by human experts. Gemma-3-27B-it, an instruction fine-tuned open-source large language model (LLM) by Google, was used, and few-shot prompting was applied to enable the generation of patient-friendly simplifications of 64 deidentified geriatric outpatient reports written in German while preserving clinical meaning. LLM-generated simplifications were compared with those produced by 2 medical experts in a blinded evaluation. Quality was assessed using three approaches: (1) embedding-based semantic similarity to the original report, (2) blinded expert review by 2 clinicians, and (3) review by patient representatives, with the latter 2 using a standardized Likert-scale questionnaire. AI-generated simplifications were comparable to geriatrician-authored simplifications regarding semantic similarity (P=.02) and were preferred by patient representatives (P<.001) as well as one expert reviewer (P=.001). Expert reviewers perceived physician-authored simplifications as more complete (P<.001), a finding that correlated with text length (P<.001). This study demonstrates the feasibility of using LLMs via few-shot prompting to simplify medical reports for improved perceived patient comprehension in geriatric care. Future prospective studies should examine whether such AI-driven simplifications positively impact objective health-related outcomes, adherence, and patient engagement.

title: An explainable, bias-audited machine learning model to detect hidden hepatitis C from region-wide real-world health records
desc: Background: Although direct-acting antivirals have transformed hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment, 25-30% of active infections in Spain remain undiagnosed. We aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning model to identify undiagnosed HCV infection using only data already recorded within the health system. Materials and Methods: We conducted a retrospective, population-based cohort study using the Andalusian Population Health Database (BPS). Individuals diagnosed with HCV between 2017 and 2024 (n=25,028) were matched, up to 10:1, to controls by birth year, sex, and health district. An Explainable Boosting Machine was trained on 2017-2022 data, with a threshold set in a 2023 validation set to guarantee [≥]60% sensitivity, then evaluated unmodified in an independent, non-matched, population-representative 2024 sample approximating real-world screening. Predictors comprised chronic-disease diagnoses and laboratory summary statistics recorded [≥]30 days before the index date; age and sex were excluded as matching variables. Predictors reflecting socioeconomic proxies or matching artefacts (pharmaceutical co-payment category, a zone-level deprivation index) were removed after explainability review. Results: In the independent test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.837 (0.826 in validation), sensitivity 63.5%, specificity 91.8%, positive predictive value 7.0%, and negative predictive value 99.6%. Leading predictors were minimum alanine aminotransferase, HIV infection, dependence on non-tobacco substances, and platelet-count statistics, forming a clinically coherent, laboratory- and comorbidity-driven profile. Conclusion: An explainable model built exclusively from routine electronic health record data can identify undiagnosed HCV infection with discrimination comparable to previously published tools, evaluated under conditions approximating true population prevalence. Bias-auditing was feasible without sacrificing interpretability, supporting a scalable, equity-conscious instrument for the final phase of HCV elimination.

title: Learning a patient world model for health system simulation in intensive care
desc: Designing healthcare strategies requires anticipating their clinical and operational consequences before implementation, a task that often relies on health system simulation. Such a simulation necessitates modeling how patient states evolve and generate care demands. However, conventional approaches typically tailor compact state transitions to a single policy question and omit history-dependent dynamics, thus requiring the redefinition of states and transitions when there is a new question that entails different clinical information. We propose to learn a patient world model from longitudinal EHRs using a neural network to provide a shared clinical representation of patient trajectories that can serve simulation questions across scenarios. Taking ICU operations as an example, we train the model on MIMIC-IV, freeze it, and couple its time-queryable predictions to shared ICU calendars, resources, and queues via scenario-specific mappings, so that one model renders admission demand, care tasks, and discharge proposals across simulations evaluating ICU bed capacity, care dispatch, and post-ICU transfer capacity. Experiments show that our model matches Markov and semi-Markov comparators in aggregate occupancy and directional responses to capacity and dispatch policies. It also reproduces policy gains from replayed observed trajectories. For patients entering the same support state from different prior trajectories, the learned representation captures a 24-h recovery difference (-6.4 predicted versus -6.7 observed percentage points), a contrast missed by compact state models, which propagates into distinct simulated care demand, queue burden, and bed use. These results indicate that a learned world model of patient dynamics has the potential to replace question-specific state models, allowing new care policies to be evaluated by reconfiguring the scenario without model rebuilding.

title: LeadWeaver: Topology-Aware Masked-Lead Modeling for Robust 12-Lead ECG Diagnosis
desc: Clinical electrocardiography is organized as a structured set of correlated leads, yet most neural ECG classifiers assume that all twelve leads are present, correctly ordered, and acquired under the same device conditions at training and deployment. We propose LeadWeaver, a topology-aware ECG representation model designed for diagnosis under missing, corrupted, or device-shifted leads. LeadWeaver represents each lead as a temporal token stream, couples leads through a fixed-plus-learned physiological lead graph, and performs masked-lead latent completion rather than waveform synthesis. A reliability router estimates which observed leads should dominate each diagnostic decision, while a consistency objective aligns complete-lead and incomplete-lead predictions. We evaluate the model on PTB-XL and CPSC-style settings using complete-input diagnosis, arbitrary missing-lead subsets, lead corruption, cross-dataset transfer, calibration, and selective prediction. The central hypothesis is that robust ECG diagnosis requires explicitly modeling both inter-lead topology and uncertainty about unavailable evidence, rather than treating missing channels as zero-valued inputs.

Evaluation of PainWaive: a consumer-grade EEG headset for remote EEG monitoring and neurofeedback research in chronic pain
desc: Affordable electroencephalography (EEG) headsets could widen access to EEG-based treatment and assessment, but require rigorous validation. We evaluated PainWaive, a custom-developed 2-channel central scalp EEG headset designed for remote EEG monitoring and neurofeedback research in chronic pain. Eighty participants completed two resting-state EEGs using PainWaive and a research-grade system (LiveAmp). Alpha, beta and theta power, and peak alpha frequency (PAF), were derived from homologous central channels. PainWaive demonstrated good-to-excellent test-retest reliability for alpha power and PAF (ICCs = 0.72–0.93), with beta and theta ranging from moderate-good (ICCs = 0.42–0.76). Across 160 home-based neurofeedback sessions in two chronic pain samples, reliability was good-to-excellent across metrics (ICCs = 0.72–0.88). Spectral-shape correlations between PainWaive and LiveAmp were excellent ( r > 0.91). Cross-device agreement was moderate-to-good for alpha power and PAF (ICCs = 0.53–0.74), but weaker for beta and theta (ICCs = 0.16–0.51). Sensitivity analyses showed alpha power and PAF were robust across choices, whereas beta and theta agreement varied by pipeline. Overall, PainWaive demonstrated reliable measurement of central scalp EEG metrics, supporting repeated within-device monitoring. Cross-device findings showed correspondence with research-grade EEG for some measures but should not be interpreted as establishing direct numerical interchangeability between systems. These findings provide a technical foundation for future remote EEG and neurofeedback studies in chronic pain.

title: Mathematical foundations of artificial intelligence in healthcare: a systematic review.
desc: [Frontiers in artificial intelligence] Artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare relies on diverse mathematical frameworks, yet their contributions to model development, evaluation, interpretability, and clinical translation remain fragmented. This systematic review synthesized the classical and emerging mathematical foundations underpinning healthcare AI and examined major methodological and application trends. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, studies published between January 2016 and June 30, 2026, were identified through systematic searches of Scopus, Google Scholar, and PubMed/MEDLINE, with searches conducted using Harzing's Publish or Perish v8 where applicable. Bibliometric analysis was performed using VOSviewer, while methodological quality was assessed using an adapted JBI-based framework and AMSTAR-2 for systematic reviews. Of 653 records identified, 147 studies met the eligibility criteria. Non-mutually exclusive mathematical-domain coding identified linear algebra in 100/147 studies (68.0%), calculus and optimization in 91/147 (61.9%), and probability and statistics in 79/147 (53.7%), highlighting their roles in data representation, learning, optimization, inference, uncertainty quantification, and validation. A separate mutually exclusive classification of dominant methodological themes identified explainable and trustworthy AI in 24/147 studies (16.3%), statistics and learning theory in 23/147 (15.6%), probability and Bayesian methods in 23/147 (15.6%), calculus and optimization in 19/147 (12.9%), and linear algebra in 15/147 (10.2%). Radiology and medical imaging were the leading healthcare application (24.3%), while classification and diagnosis were the most frequent clinical task (17.1%). Overall, healthcare AI is supported by an interconnected mathematical ecosystem. Emerging approaches, including graph neural networks, Transformers, and quantum machine learning, require stronger external validation, standardized benchmarking, and rigorous evaluation for reliable clinical translation.

title: A Cross-Dataset Audit of Discrimination and Conformal Prediction Coverage in Keystroke-Based Parkinson's Disease Classi cation
desc: Typing dynamics are being investigated as a digital behavioral marker for Parkinson's disease (PD), but the cross-dataset reliability of typing-based classi ers remains uncertain. We evaluated four public datasets (475 par ticipants; 270 with PD and 205 controls) across 12 transfer directions using split conformal prediction targeting 90% marginal coverage. In all three pri mary directions, coverage was below the 0.90 target and the one-sided tests remained signi cant after Holm correction: 0.598 (95% CI, 0.4830.704) for Tappy[->]MIT, 0.850 (0.7880.899) for MIT[->]Tappy, and 0.732 (0.6840.777) for clinical[->]self-reported transfer. Discrimination and coverage did not con sistently change together: LightGBM had lower AUC than logistic regression in all 12 directions but higher coverage in 11, with larger prediction sets. Class-conditional coverage varied by target cohort: PD-conditional cover age was 0.214 for Tappy[->]MIT, whereas healthy-control coverage was 0.700 for MIT[->]Tappy and 0.627 for clinical[->]self-reported transfer. Recalibration with 9 and 18 labeled target participants raised the lower condence bound above 0.80 in the latter two directions; in Tappy[->]MIT, it remained below 0.80 even with 25 labels. Weighted conformal prediction yielded coverage of 0.9181.000 without target labels but returned the full label set for 86% 100% of participants. Stress tests did not reproduce the observed coverage patterns, and black-box shift estimation did not support pure label shift as the dominant explanation for Tappy[->]MIT. Evaluating typing dynamics as a digital marker for PD requires cross-dataset assessment of discrimination, marginal and class-conditional coverage, and recovery costs. Clinical screen ing utility has not been established.

title: OraRefer: Segmentation-Guided Multi-Photograph Fusion for Oral Cancer Screening with Guaranteed Patient-Level Sensitivity
desc: Oral cancer and the oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMD) that can precede it are visible on the oral mucosa, which makes smartphone photographs a promising tool for screening. Deep learning models for this task classify individual photographs. However, screening refers patients, not photographs: a patient is usually photographed several times, and the referral decision must miss no more than a set share of patients with disease. We propose OraRefer, a patient-level screening model that reads each photograph with a segmentation-guided foundation model that conditions its class decision on the predicted lesion, combines all photographs of a patient with risk factors, and refers through a threshold with a finite-sample sensitivity guarantee. The model localizes the mouth itself, so inference needs no annotation. On 3000 photographs of 714 patients, patient-level fusion reaches an AUROC of 0.919 and outperforms attention-based multiple-instance learning. At a 90% sensitivity target, OraRefer detects 95% of patients with OPMD or cancer and misses 3 of 61 patients with cancer, at a specificity of 0.610. Because the threshold is calibrated without retraining, each clinic can set its own guaranteed operating point on a local calibration sample.

title: Hierarchical Temporal Transformer for Cancer Grade Prediction and Cross-Cancer Transfer Learning from Pathology Reports
desc: Background: Language models for cancer reports usually read one document at a time and are tested on tumour types seen in training. Continuous-time sequence models address the first gap, but whether they use visit timing, not just order, is seldom tested. Methods: We developed the Hierarchical Temporal Transformer (HTT), which encodes reports with adapted BiomedBERT and reads the sequence with a cancer-type-conditioned temporal transformer. We evaluated it against best-possible AUROC ceilings on two synthetic benchmarks, one with the label stated in the text and one recoverable only from tumour sizes and visit intervals (ten seeds). Diagnostics led to an interval-aware time code (HTT-IA). On 4,786 TCGA pathology reports in 14 types, three types were withheld, and a text-only HTT was compared with a survival model. Results: On the phrase benchmark HTT reached AUROC 0.931 +/- 0.012 against 0.913 +/- 0.007 for a last-report baseline (+0.018, 95% CI -0.009 to +0.050); dates cannot raise the ceiling there. On the growth benchmark the initial time code scored 0.790, equal to a no-time model (0.787), whereas HTT-IA reached 0.843 (+0.053, 0.026 to 0.082) against ceilings of 0.894 without and 0.979 with dates. On unseen tumour types HTT reached 0.925 +/- 0.007, equal to in-distribution performance and to a single-report baseline. Text-only macro C-index was 0.592 (CALM 0.626-0.652). Conclusion: Cross-type transfer is carried by the pre-trained encoder. Visit timing is used only when the data make it identifiable and the time code is on a clinical scale. Ceilings, order-only ablations and re-dating probes are inexpensive checks for such models.

title: Beyond Artificial Intelligence: Vocation and the Sacred Relationship Between Physician and Patient.
desc: [The Linacre quarterly] The role of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine should be discussed following Pope Leo XIV's recent encyclical on AI and the need to protect human dignity in this era of advancing technology. As a result of its efficiency and accessibility to people for medical advice, AI is already starting to change healthcare. These advances may improve patient care, but medicine is about more than access to information. Medicine is a vocation motivated by the compassionate service to others, and this must be defended. Using the teachings of Antiqua et Nova and Magnifica Humanitas as a guide, this commentary discusses how Catholic bioethics can contribute to the integration of AI in clinical practice. These ethical principles can direct the proper use of AI while still upholding physicians' responsibilities to their patients. Physicians must recognize each patient's dignity and needs, which go beyond the knowledge that any algorithm can offer. Furthermore, the recommendations that these AI systems provide are only as strong as the information available to them, emphasizing the continued importance of the physician's clinical judgment. As we continue to monitor the emergence and growth of AI, the Church serves as a reminder to us that AI should support physicians' clinical judgment while preserving the sacred relationship of trust between physician and patient.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Heterogeneous Cognitive and Biomedical Knowledge Graphs: The Role of Graph Grounding in Multi-Hop Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation
desc: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in biomedical and cognitive neuroscience, but their ability to reason reliably over heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs) remains unclear. We benchmark five LLMs (GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT) across five KGs: DrugBank, NeuroSynth, Cognitive Atlas, Brain Map, and GDPKG. We introduce a multitier query dataset to evaluate reasoning depth and factual accuracy under KG-aware (graph-grounded) and KG-agnostic conditions. Inter-annotator agreement was substantial, with Cohen's kappa of 0.781 (range: 0.753-0.807) and Fleiss' kappa of 0.77. Results show that general-purpose models, particularly GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.0 Pro, generally outperform domain-specific models on multi-hop and high-level reasoning tasks, although performance declines as query complexity increases. KG grounding reduces hallucination rates across all evaluated models. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, domain-specific models do not consistently outperform general-purpose models on specialized tasks without graph grounding. These findings highlight the value of combining broad language-model capabilities with structured domain knowledge. We provide practical guidance for selecting LLM-KG integration strategies based on task complexity and computational constraints, and discuss hybrid neurosymbolic architectures for personalized medicine, cognitive disorder diagnosis, and explainable AI.

title: pLM-bVAE: protein language model-enhanced binary representation improves quantum annealing-based protein sequence design
desc: Quantum annealing (QA) has been explored as an approach for protein design in vast combinatorial sequence spaces. Applying QA to protein sequence design requires amino acid sequences to be encoded as binary vectors, and optimized vectors to be decoded back into amino acid sequences. Thus, both the quality of binary encoding and sequence reconstruction accuracy are important for effective QA-based optimization. Binary variational autoencoder (bVAE) has been used to map protein sequences to binary representations in QA-based protein sequence design. However, bVAE was originally developed for natural language modeling, and its suitability for proteins has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we present pLM-bVAE, which incorporates protein representations derived from a pretrained protein language model (pLM) into the original bVAE model. In computational experiments on three public protein variant datasets, pLM-bVAE showed higher sequence reconstruction accuracy and binary encoding performance than bVAE. Moreover, we incorporated pLM-bVAE into a QA-based protein sequence design framework. Across all three datasets, pLM-bVAE generated more high-scoring sequences with greater sequence dissimilarity from the training and validation data than bVAE. Our results demonstrate that pLM-bVAE provides an effective binary representation for improving QA-based protein sequence design. Availability The source code used in this manuscript is available at https://github.com/hueda8/pLM-bVAE.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Bridge to Gaps in Delirium Prediction, Detection, and Management.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
desc: [Journal of the American Geriatrics Society] Delirium affects up to one-third of hospitalized older adults and is associated with adverse outcomes. Despite its clinical importance and the availability of validated screening tools, current care gaps extend beyond under-recognition to inconsistent risk stratification, workforce constraints, documentation burden, fragmented intervention delivery, and practical challenges with monitoring of response. We review how artificial intelligence (AI) could bridge these gaps and distinguish model development and validation, real-world clinical implementation, and emerging concepts in delirium care. Prediction models leveraging multimodal health record data, including structured variables and unstructured clinical notes, report good discrimination for delirium risk stratification, but only a few models have been integrated into clinical practice. A live multimodal machine learning model increased targeted delirium detection, yet a pre-post comparative study found a longer length of stay; improved recognition alone therefore does not equate with improved outcomes. Natural language processing, large language models, computer vision, ambient sensing, and wearable technologies enable more continuous, objective, and less labor-intensive assessment compared with traditional screening methods, but evidence remains limited with concerns about false positives and generalizability. AI-supported delirium management through reinforcement learning and digital twins is currently largely conceptual. Responsible AI adoption requires a clearly defined intended use, external validation, action pathways, equitable performance, privacy and security, consent and transparency, clinician oversight, patient preferences, and post-deployment monitoring. AI is most defensible as an adjunct that connects evidence-based delirium care to reliable execution rather than as a replacement for clinical assessment. Prospective comparative studies should evaluate patient outcomes, resource use, and balancing measures.

title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
desc: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

title: Agentic AI enables cell segmentation-free cell-type inference and cell-type-guided cell segmentation in spatial transcriptomics
desc: Cell-type identification in spatial transcriptomics often relies on cell segmentation, which can introduce inaccuracies in cell boundaries and transcript assignment. Segmentation-free or cell-free methods have been developed to completely avoid cell segmentation, but inaccurate cell typing hinder accurate downstream analysis. Here, we introduce SSAF-T, a segmentation-free agentic framework that identifies cell types directly from spatial gene expression without predefined reference datasets. For the reference-free cell typing, SSAF-T incorporates CeLLMan, which employs expert-level agents for each organ to annotate cell types using a literature-grounded knowledge graph. We benchmark SSAF-T on both array-based and imaging-based spatial transcriptomics datasets in terms of accuracy, reproducibility, and scalability. We further show that SSAF-T provides an accurate cell segmentation based on the segmentation-free mapping, which ensure compatibility to existing downstream analysis ecosystem, and eventually enable quantitative analysis at single-cell level.

Development and Validation of a Multimodal Deep Learning Model Using Peripheral Oxygen Saturation and Ballistocardiography Signals for Predicting Apnea-Hypopnea Index in Obstructive Sleep Apnea
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Fu Jen Catholic University; conditions: Obstructive Sleep Apnea; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 100; status: RECRUITING] Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common sleep disorder associated with cardiovascular, metabolic, and neurocognitive complications. The standard diagnostic test for OSA is in-laboratory polysomnography (PSG), which can be costly, labor-intensive, and inconvenient for repeated or large-scale screening. Therefore, there is a need for a convenient and non-invasive method to help identify individuals who may be at risk for OSA. This prospective observational study aims to develop and clinically validate a multimodal deep learning model that integrates peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO₂) signals and ballistocardiography (BCG) data collected using a smart mattress system to estimate the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI). Adult participants undergoing routine overnight PSG for suspected OSA will be enrolled. During sleep, synchronized SpO₂ and BCG signals will be recorded non-invasively. The performance of the deep learning model will be evaluated by comparing the predicted AHI values with AHI values derived from PSG. This study seeks to evaluate whether this practical, non-invasive, and scalable approach may support early identification of OSA risk and improve access to sleep disorder assessment in both clinical and home-based settings.

title: Artificial intelligence for vascular minimally invasive surgery: techniques, clinical integration, and challenges.
desc: [Frontiers in cardiovascular medicine] Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.

title: LLM-Assisted Label Noise Correction for EEG-Based Sleep Stage Classification
desc: Automatic sleep stage classification from electroencephalography (EEG) signals is a critical task in clinical sleep medicine. While deep learning models have shown promising results in this domain, their performance is fundamentally constrained by the quality of training labels, which human experts manually annotate and that are subject to inter-rater disagreement and systematic labeling errors. In this paper, we propose a novel LLM-assisted label-noise filtering pipeline that operates exclusively during training to identify and remove unreliable sleep-stage annotations before retraining the classifier. Specifically, TinySleepNet is first trained on the original dataset to extract per-epoch SoftMax confidence scores, then low-confidence epochs are submitted to LLaMA 3.1 along with their EEG spectral features and surrounding sequence context. The LLM evaluates each epoch against AASM sleep-scoring guidelines and assigns a verdict of RELIABLE or SUSPICIOUS. Suspicious epochs are removed from the training set, and TinySleepNet is retrained on the cleaned data. Evaluated on the Sleep-EDF Expanded dataset using 20-fold cross-validation, our method improves overall accuracy from 81.8% to 84.6% and Macro F1-score from 75.6% to 77.4%, with particularly notable gains in REM detection. Crucially, because the LLM operates only during training, the lightweight TinySleepNet architecture (1.3M parameters) is preserved at inference, making the proposed pipeline suitable for real-time, wearable sleep monitoring applications.

title: Generative Models for Novel Enzymatic Reactions: How Far Do They Go?
desc: Enzyme function prediction is a long-standing problem in biology, and deep learning methods have recently become popular to improve performance on this task. While most of these models focus on classifying enzymes or mapping them to known reactions, predicting unknown biochemical reactions remains underexplored. Here we thoroughly examine an approach that generates reactions absent from the training data from the enzyme alone. Existing methods such as BLASTp or CLIPZyme cannot, by design, output reactions that are absent from their training data or were not supplied at inference. The closest prior model, RxnPred, reports high fingerprint-similarity scores on held-out enzymes, a less stringent criterion than exact recovery, but fails to recover the correct answer on unseen reactions. We present a structure-conditioned generative model that outputs a complete reaction, reactants and products, and evaluate it on EnzymeMap_x, a reaction-disjoint benchmark in which no test reaction appears in training, under exact, stereo-respecting scoring. On this benchmark, within 400 sampled candidates, the model generates the complete, correct reaction for 25.0% of the subset of test enzyme--reaction pairs whose reaction is a new combination of metabolites seen in training. Surprisingly, it also correctly generates a few reactions composed of metabolites it has not seen in training (1.6%), though their embeddings are present in the vocabulary. With a lower budget, re-ranking places the correct reaction first for 5.6% of pairs and in the top ten for 12.4%, when the reaction is assumed not to be already known (0.2% and 8.1% without that assumption) along with confidence scores. Assessed more leniently, the model produces at least one correct reaction known for the enzyme (usually memorised from training) for 71.2% of test pairs. Going further, without any retraining, a sequence-only model given the reactants as well as the enzyme produces the correct product set for 9.5% of pairs within five candidates, without re-ranking. We also present head-to-head comparisons on these tasks with BLASTp, DIAMOND, RxnPred and Horizyn. Structure conditioning improves fingerprint similarity on homology-stratified splits, but a matched sequence-only ablation at the best configuration finds no measurable effect on exact recovery. Data coverage and chemical initialisation of the vocabulary seem to matter more than encoder geometry.

Deep learning optimisation for cardiology: Neural Architecture Search-driven arrhythmia classification with electrocardiograms.
desc: [PloS one] Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. Sudden cardiac death (SCD) accounts for roughly 50% of all cardiac deaths. The electrocardiogram (ECG) is widely used for diagnosing cardiac disease. However, the complexity of interpretation limits the ECG's efficacy. Modern deep learning methods can assist clinicians in diagnosis. We applied Neural Architecture Search (NAS) to identify optimal deep learning architectures for classifying cardiac arrhythmias with ECGs. We applied the Differentiable Architecture Search strategy to an AutoFormer search and trained, validated, and tested the resulting model on the PhysioNet Challenge 2021 (PC21) dataset (n = 88,253 from three continents). We optimised hyperparameters on the NAS output, exploring input patch size, class weighting, and loss function. The PC21 metric and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) are the performance metrics. The NAS converged towards minimal architectural configurations (embedding dimension: 384, depth: 4, self-attention heads: 4, MLP ratio: 1) with a validation and test PC21 metric of 0.66 (PC21 winner: 0.63). The NAS-created network achieved an AUROC of 0.97 and a PC21 metric of 0.72 during testing (PC21 winner: 0.69). We tested the PC21 winner architecture (1D-convolutional neural network with attention mechanism) without the attention mechanism and with the NAS-suggested architecture of 4 self-attention heads (instead of 8). The architecture without the attention mechanism performed similarly to the one with 8 self-attention heads (AUROC: 0.90, PC21 metric: 0.69). The architecture with 4 self-attention heads scored an AUROC of 0.91 and improved the PC21 metric to 0.71. The attention mechanism visualisation for two SCD-related arrhythmias (premature ventricular contractions and prolonged QT-interval) showed more clinically relevant attention for the 4-self-attention-head architectures. We interpret architectural simplicity as driving performance in arrhythmia classification. The self-attention mechanism can autonomously abstract clinical representations, simplifying clinical deployment by eliminating the need for an explicit feature-extraction pipeline.

title: USB Gym: A Gymnasium Testbed for Closed-Loop Ultrasound View Matching
desc: Background and Objective: Our main goal is ultrasound guidance: moving a probe until its image matches a target view. Published methods for each part of a guide are evaluated in separate simulators. We asked whether these methods, combined into one guide, are good enough. Methods: We built USB Gym, a testbed whose standard engine simulates ultrasound from public patient CT, with a network drawing organ textures from CT labels. Its guide has three replaceable parts (slots), an organ segmenter, a controller and a reward, which received 20 published methods, each run on the same 60 episodes of six held-out patients. In each slot, a published method replaced ours only if detectably better on these patients. The better of this combination and our original guide on 20 new CTs is the benchmark baseline. A pose oracle, reading the exact probe pose available only in simulation, set the reference. The results below are exploratory. Results: On these CTs, the probe started on average 16.0 mm from the target view; the pose oracle brought it to 1.5 mm. Of the results known when the combination was fixed, only an image-similarity reward (SSIM) was slightly but detectably better, so the combination was our guide with that reward. This combination was the benchmark baseline, ending at 13.7 mm (16% of the oracle's progress). Conclusions: Combining untuned published methods with ours did not guide the probe near the target view; the task remains under-explored. The testbed accepts new methods; no guide was tested on hardware.

title: Bioprocess Modeling Made Easy With Hybrax
desc: Hybrid models that embed neural networks in ordinary differential equations are increasingly popular in bioprocess modeling, but they are challenging to set up. Much of the effort goes into the code around the model: wet-lab data must be imported and pre-processed, feeds and sampling must be accounted for in the balance equations, and a training loop with cross-validation must be set up. Researchers usually write this code from scratch for each project. In addition, no widely adopted format for bioprocess data exists, and datasets are mostly published in bespoke spreadsheets or not at all. As a result, models and datasets from the literature are difficult to reproduce, reuse, or compare.We present Hybrax, an open-source Python framework that addresses these problems. It combines a flexible format for bioprocess data with a customizable end-to-end training pipeline for mechanistic and hybrid models. Hybrax derives the transport terms in the process dynamics automatically and provides the utilities needed for training, so that researchers can focus on developing the model itself. It also facilitates model sharing and reproducibility: each training checkpoint contains the model parameters, code, configuration, and training data required to run the model or retrain it from scratch. We demonstrate Hybrax by re-implementing two models from the literature, one trained on real-world E. coli data and one on synthetic HEK293 data, with performance comparable to the original models. Hybrax is available at https://github.com/hybrax/hybrax.

Machine Learning in Smart Hydrogel 4D Printing: Advances, Challenges, and Translational Perspectives.
desc: [Annals of biomedical engineering] The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and smart hydrogel-based additive manufacturing offers new capabilities for fabricating adaptive structures, though the field remains in early stages of translation. Smart hydrogels, with their stimuli-responsive properties and biocompatibility, present opportunities in tissue engineering, drug delivery, and soft robotics. However, the complexity of their material behavior and the challenges of high-resolution four-dimensional (4D) printing demand advanced computational approaches to optimize design, processing, and performance. This review systematically examines the role of AI, encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and generative models, in addressing these challenges. We critically assess AI-driven strategies for hydrogel formulation, real-time process control, structural optimization, and biological outcome prediction, distinguishing between retrospectively fitted models and prospectively validated implementations. A key contribution of this review is the clear differentiation between AI-assisted 3D printing and genuine 4D printing, where constructs exhibit time-dependent shape change, actuation, or degradation in response to stimuli. We introduce AI applications in specific hydrogel printing domains, provide a comparative framework for distinguishing 3D from 4D systems, and critically evaluate quantitative claims with attention to dataset size, validation approaches, and reproducibility. Case studies highlight where AI enhances printability, resolution, and functional outcomes, while we also identify persistent limitations including data scarcity, model interpretability, and regulatory hurdles. A comparative analysis of AI-assisted versus traditional design-of-experiment strategies reveals that while AI offers advantages in high-dimensional spaces, traditional methods remain more accessible, interpretable, and reproducible for simpler systems. By synthesizing recent advancements with transparent methodology and practical guidance, this study provides a roadmap for future research at the intersection of AI and smart hydrogel additive manufacturing, advocating for interdisciplinary collaboration and standardized reporting to enable next-generation innovations.

title: Multimodal Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Modeling
desc: Medical 3D scans and reports are inherently hierarchical, with diagnostic cues concentrated in specific anatomical regions across multiple levels of organization. Yet, most medical vision-language models ignore this structure and fail to focus on clinically relevant anatomy. We introduce MedHiVE, which combines hierarchical vision-language Soft Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) with contrastive learning to jointly model fine-grained anatomy and global scan context. To our knowledge, MedHiVE is the first framework to route both vision and text tokens through a two-level SMoE hierarchy organized by anatomical scale, coupling this with report-derived anatomy-level contrastive alignment for 3D medical imaging. This replaces the direct region-text alignment of statically pooled features and vision-only hierarchical routing of prior work with dynamic, slot-based cross-modal information flow across anatomical scales. MedHiVE operates via a two-level, learnable token-routing mechanism, where local image and text features are first routed through a local SMoE and then fused by a global SMoE into unified multimodal representations. Contrastive learning aligns both anatomy-level and global vision-language representations in a unified space. Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision, MedHiVE consistently surpasses 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets on 3 tasks: segmentation, classification, and detection, demonstrating the importance of hierarchical modeling. The code for MedHiVE is at github.com/szczurek-lab/MedHiVE.

Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Detection and Characterization of Colorectal Polyps during Colonoscopy: Evidence and Future Perspectives.
desc: [Gut and liver] Colonoscopy is central to colorectal cancer prevention because it enables early detection and removal of premalignant lesions. However, lesions can still be missed, and endoscopic differentiation of neoplastic from nonneoplastic polyps remains variable, particularly for diminutive lesions. The potential of artificial intelligence (AI) as a supportive technology for improving both polyp detection and characterization during colonoscopy has therefore been investigated. Since early studies of convolutional neural network-based computer-aided detection (CADe), the focus has shifted from retrospective image-based validation to real-time randomized trials, meta-analyses, and clinical guideline discussions. Accumulating evidence suggests that CADe improves surrogate detection outcomes, including the adenoma detection rate (ADR), polyp detection rate, adenomas per colonoscopy, and adenoma miss rate. Although a higher ADR is associated with a lower risk of postcolonoscopy colorectal cancer, it remains unknown whether the incremental improvement in the ADR achieved by CADe translates into lower postcolonoscopy colorectal cancer incidence or colorectal cancer-related mortality. Recent multicenter data further support the effectiveness of real-time CADe systems in improving detection-related outcomes, while also indicating that benefit varies with lesion characteristics and user experience. In parallel, computer-aided diagnosis (CADx) has been developed to assist the optical characterization of colorectal polyps, particularly for diminutive lesions and potential resect-and-discard or diagnose-and-leave strategies. CADx systems using white-light imaging and structured high-confidence diagnostic rules show promise, but the clinical implementation of CADx remains less mature than that of CADe. This review summarizes current evidence for AI-assisted polyp detection and characterization and discusses limitations and future directions for integrating CADe and CADx into human-centered colonoscopy practices.

title: Interpretable Multimodal MRI-Clinical Fusion for Functional Outcome Prediction After Acute Ischemic Stroke
desc: This study evaluates the added prognostic value of day-1 multimodal MRI for predicting three-month functional outcome after acute ischemic stroke (AIS). Sixty-six AIS patients with ADC, DWI, FLAIR, and clinical data were analyzed. Three-dimensional pretrained ResNet embeddings were extracted from each MRI modality, reduced using fold-isolated principal component analysis, and combined with structured clinical variables and ADC-derived lesion biomarkers. Linear support vector machines were evaluated using eight-fold stratified group cross-validation across MRI modality combinations. Clinical-only modeling achieved strong performance (AUC = $0.899 \pm 0.151$), while MRI-only models showed limited discrimination (AUC $\approx$ $0.67$-$0.73$). Among multimodal configurations, FLAIR-clinical fusion achieved the highest mean cross-validated performance (AUC = $0.948 \pm 0.061$), followed by ADC-clinical fusion (AUC = $0.941 \pm 0.094$). Full ADC-DWI-FLAIR fusion did not consistently outperform single-modality clinical fusion. Feature-importance analysis identified age, NIHSS subscores, ADC lesion burden, and learned FLAIR representations as key contributors, while qualitative FLAIR activation maps showed responses over lesion-like regions. These findings suggest that compact day-1 FLAIR and ADC representations provide complementary prognostic information beyond clinical variables and support interpretable, data-efficient outcome prediction in AIS.
